full_judgment: 33. Before I part with the case, I think it necessary and expedient to put on record that there is a wrong notion in currency in the society regarding the legal incidence of the fine imposed by a criminal Court upon an accused person. While convicting an accused, the trial Court very often imposes a fit upon the accused in addition to awarding a sentence of imprisonment. In default of payment of the fine, the accused is made to suffer imprisonment for a further period fixed by the Court. It must be clearly understood by all concerned that the fine imposed by the Criminal Court upon an accused is of the nature of a financial punishment as distinguished from physical punishment and it must be realised from him under all normal circumstances. The accused has no option in the matter to plead that he would prefer to suffer imprisonment for a fixed term in lieu of payment of the fine, fine being compulsory payment having the force of a civil Court decree under section 386 of the Code of Criminal. Procedure if the accused is allowed to avoid the payment of the fine by opting to undergo imprisonment for a fixed term in default of payment of the fine, the very legislative intent for imposition of the fine shall stand negatived. The imposition of the fine by a Criminal Court upon the accused as a financial punishment is meant for prompt realisation of the fine as a public due in a summary way under the provisions of section 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure without the necessity of initiating an independent, time-consuming and cumbersome proceeding. This is why in a case under the Anti-Corruption laws, an accused is sentenced to pay a fine equivalent to the amount of money or the value of the goods misappropriated by him in addition to the substantive sentence of imprisonment warranted by the offences involved in the case. If the accused is allowed to exercise his option in the matter of payment of the fine, the relevant public authority or body suffering financial injury at the instance of the accused shall be left with no prompt and easy measure for realisation of its losses from the accused, who enriched himself at the expense of the aggrieved. This will tantamount to giving a premium to the delinquent at the cost of the expropriated. The fine is thus a charge upon the assets of the convict as a public due and it continues to be so even after his death and it must be recovered with utmost promptitude. It is only when the assets of the convict are not sufficient to cover the amount of the fine, he shall then suffer imprisonment for default to pay the fine and not otherwise on any pretext. A duty is thus cast upon the trial Court to take urgent steps for realisation of the fine imposed upon the accused and it must ensure that it does not lapse by any sort of inaction and laches on its part.
